Egalitarian
ē-găl-ĭ-târ´ĭ-an
n. and adj. (in theology, one holding that no office or authority in church or home is restricted by sex)
French égalitaire, from égal, equal. In evangelical usage the word names the position set against complementarianism; both terms date from the 1980s, though the dispute is older.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Egalitarianism holds that Scripture assigns no permanent functional distinction between men and women in church office or in marriage. Its central text is “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal 3:28), read together with the women who plainly laboured in the apostolic churches — Phebe a servant of the church (Rom 16:1), Priscilla instructing Apollos (Act 18:26), Philip's four daughters which did prophesy (Act 21:9). The complementarian reply rests on the restriction and its stated ground: “I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man… For Adam was first formed, then Eve” (1Ti 2:12–13), and on “the head of the woman is the man” (1Co 11:3).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry for egalitarian, the word being later than his dictionary; he defines equality as an agreement of things in dimensions, quantity, or quality; likeness; the same degree of dignity or claims.

expand to see more

EQUALITY, n. An agreement of things in dimensions, quantity or quality; likeness; similarity in regard to two things compared.

2. The same degree of dignity or claims.

3. Evenness; uniformity; sameness in state or continued course.

4. Evenness; plainness; uniformity; as an equality of surface.

Key Scripture

Gal 3:28 — "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus."

1Ti 2:12 — "But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence."

1Ti 2:13 — "For Adam was first formed, then Eve."

1Co 11:3 — "But I would have you know, that the head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God."

Eph 5:25 — "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;"

Act 18:26 — "And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly."

Modern Corruption

Equality of worth and identity of role are treated as the same claim, and Galatians 3:28 answers the first question without addressing the second.

expand to see more

Galatians 3:28 is the hinge, and the context settles what it is arguing. Paul is not describing church order; he is concluding an argument about who may be justified by faith and inherit the promise made to Abraham — the verse ends ye are all one in Christ Jesus, and the next verse draws the conclusion: then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise. It abolishes every distinction as a ground of standing before God, and it does so in three pairs. If it abolished role along with standing, it would abolish the distinction between slave and free as thoroughly as that between male and female, and the same apostle goes on giving instructions to both.

The complementarian position stands or falls on the reason Paul attaches to the restriction. Had he grounded 1 Timothy 2:12 in the culture of Ephesus, or in the education of women, or in a local disorder, the restriction would expire with its cause; he grounds it instead in the order of creation — for Adam was first formed, then Eve — which does not expire, and in Genesis 2, which precedes the fall. That is why the argument cannot be settled by showing that women prophesied, served, taught other women, instructed Apollos privately, or carried the epistle to the Romans. All of that is in the text, and none of it is the office in question.

There is a corruption on the complementarian side, and it is uglier than the exegetical error it opposes. Ephesians 5 gives the husband a single verb repeated three times — love, as Christ loved the church and gave himself for it — and a headship defined by crucifixion. A man who quotes 1 Timothy 2 to secure his own comfort, who treats his wife's judgment as an obstacle rather than a gift, or who calls domination order, has taken the half of the doctrine that costs him nothing. The Bible's complementarianism is not a division of privileges; it is a division of sacrifices, and the heavier one falls on the head.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek arsen (G730) and thelu (G2338), male and female; authenteo (G831), to usurp authority; kephale (G2776), head; hupotasso (G5293), to submit.

expand to see more

Greek ouk eni arsen kai thelu (G730, G2338) — there is neither male nor female; Galatians 3:28.

Greek authenteo (G831) — to exercise or usurp authority over; 1 Timothy 2:12 only.

Greek kephale (G2776) — head; 1 Corinthians 11:3, Ephesians 5:23; hupotasso (G5293), Ephesians 5:22, 5:24, 1 Peter 3:1.

Usage

"“Neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus” — three pairs, and a question about standing."

"“For Adam was first formed, then Eve” — the reason given, and it precedes the fall."

"“As Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it” — the half that costs the head everything."
